title: TC3-21502
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): He is appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated May 1, 2023.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal.
The Appellant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of India. He is appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated May 1, 2023.

The Appellant alleges fear of persecution in India from an individual, SC, along with powerful politicians and the police. The Appellant alleges he submitted a complaint to the police which he then escalated to higher authorities, including the Prime Minister's Office, for SC's failure to repay a loan. The Appellant then alleges SC and his men physically attacked him because he had filed the above complaint to the police.

The Appellant also alleges he and his family have been constantly subjected to persecution based on their membership in a scheduled caste community. The Appellant alleges he made complaints to the police and was assaulted by goons. The Appellant alleges that because he is of a lower caste than SC, he was being forced to take back his complaint against him.

The Appellant fled to Canada arriving on XXXX XXXX, 2019, and made a claim for refugee protection in February 2020. Since his arrival in Canada, the Appellant alleges his brother received death threats from goons and the police.
The determinative issue before the RPD was credibility. The RPD found the Appellant failed to credibly establish the central allegations underlying his claim.
The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its credibility analysis, oversimplified the evidence, and failed to look at the forward-facing risk of persecution.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
No new evidence was tendered or admitted nor was there a request for an oral hearing.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1

I find the Appellant's alleged fear has a nexus to the Convention ground of membership in a particular social group, namely a lower caste. I have therefore assessed this appeal under both s. 96 and s. 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (Act).

From my independent review of the evidence on record, the determinative issue before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is that the Appellant failed to provide persuasive evidence to establish his allegations of persecution under s. 96 or harm under section 97(1) of the Act. Credibility

As indicated above, the determinative issue before the RPD was credibility. The Court in Maldonado stated that, "When an applicant swears to the truth of certain allegations, this creates a presumption that those allegations are true unless there be reason to doubt their truthfulness."2 However, this presumption does not extend to speculations or inferences. The Federal Court has stated that, "...this is only a presumption and does not apply when there is reason to doubt the truthfulness of an applicant's statements."3 I accept some of the Appellant's allegations as credible, except where I find them to be speculation as outlined in paragraph 32 below. Attack is established
The RPD made a negative inference regarding the Appellant's credibility based on inconsistencies in the Appellant's evidence regarding the date of his alleged attack.

The Appellant argues that the RPD's findings relied on a microscopic analysis of the evidence to justify negative credibility findings and did not give sufficient weight to the medical report which corroborated the attack.

From my analysis of the evidence record, I find that despite the inconsistencies in the Appellant's evidence regarding the date of the alleged attack, the medical report does corroborate the attack. I agree with the Appellant that the purpose of a medical report is not to identify the perpetrators of the attack. The injuries outlined in the report are consistent with the attack described by the Appellant and I do not agree with the RPD that the inconsistencies regarding the date of the attack are enough to rebut the presumption of truth set out in Maldonado.

However, the question that arises is whether this one attack, based on a personal vendetta, by SC and unidentified goons, and pursuant unresolved complaints filed by the Appellant, amount to persecution or a danger of torture, a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. It is my finding that they do not. This is why the determinative issue is not credibility, but rather the insufficiency of evidence.

In this case, I find there is insufficient evidence to show either caste discrimination amounting to persecution, or criminal activity amounting to cruel treatment or threats to the Appellant's life. Section 96 risk of persecution is not established
The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant was not persecuted because he is of a lower caste than SC.
The Appellant argues the RPD did not consider the forward-looking risk the Appellant faces, given the country conditions evidence.

Based on my independent review of the evidence record, I find that the RPD correctly assessed the evidence available regarding the Appellant's caste identity, and its determination that the Appellant's caste identity was one which would not subject him to a serious possibility of forward-looking persecution is the correct one.

Even though the Indian Constitution specifically prohibits discrimination on the grounds of caste, the National Documentation Package (NDP) for India indicates that "Dalits and other people considered to be of a low caste face a high risk of official and societal discrimination, including social segregation, exclusion, compromised access to education and health care".4 There is also evidence that dominant castes will not allow "their children to play with Dalits or to be in a relationship with a Dalit".5

There is also information in the NDP that Dalits are customarily relegated to the bottom of the caste hierarchy and confined to livelihood tasks viewed as deplorable or deemed too menial by higher caste groups. Their caste-designated occupation reinforces the social stigma that they are unclean or "untouchable" and perpetuates widespread discrimination.6 The objective documentary evidence states that "[a] majority of Dalits are still prevented from owning land and are forced to live on the outskirts of villages, often on barren land. While the struggle for Dalit land rights is growing, land reforms intended to benefit the rural poor and Dalits have been ineffective due to weak legislative provisions, inadequate implementation, and a lack of State commitment".7

While the documentation reflects caste-based discrimination remains an issue in India, I find that the evidence before me does not demonstrate that all lower caste members face a serious possibility of persecution in India. For discrimination against a person to amount to persecution, it must be serious and occur with repetition and must have consequences of a prejudicial nature for the person, such as when an individual is denied a core human right, or such as the right to practice religion or to earn a livelihood.8

My review of the evidence indicates that the Appellant's experiences do not meet this threshold. At no point in the past has the Appellant been denied a core human right or been disadvantaged economically or socially in India nor is there sufficient evidence to demonstrate that he risks being denied these rights in the future. In fact, the Appellant has had 18 years of education, including a XXXX degree from India and a XXXX degree from the United Kingdom. The Appellant has also secured excellent employment opportunities in the Middle East and the United Kingdom. The Appellant was in a financial position to lend SC money despite being a member of a lower caste.

There is also no evidence in this case that demonstrates the Appellant is suffering from segregation due to his caste identity. The Appellant testified that he and SC played together as children and their parents were good friends.9 The Appellant also testified that both of SC's brothers agree SC should repay him.10 The Appellant clarified in his testimony that he was never directly threatened by the MLA who mediated the dispute with SC.11 There is also no evidence that any members of the Appellant's family, presumably members of the same lower caste, have been harmed in any way.

The Appellant cites the 1990 case of Salibian which states, "the best evidence that an individual faces a serious chance of persecution is usually the treatment afforded similarly situation persons in the country of origin".12 However, more recent jurisprudence has consistently found that "it is not sufficient to point to general human rights problems in a country without providing evidence as to how those problems have impacted, or will impact, the claimants".13 I find the Appellant's evidence has not demonstrated the impact the country conditions have had or will have on him going forward.

Based on the above analysis, I find that the RPD was correct to find that there was insufficient evidence to establish that there is a serious possibility that the Appellant would face persecution based on his caste identity if he were to return to India. Section 97 risk of harm is not established

The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that powerful politicians and police are not trying to eliminate the Appellant and there is insufficient evidence to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that SC, along with powerful politicians and the police, will target him for a personal vendetta pursuant to section 97(1). I agree.
The Appellant argues the RPD's findings on this issue are vague and oversimplify the situation faced by the Appellant.

I am not persuaded by the Appellant's arguments. While I may agree that SC had a personal vendetta against the Appellant which likely instigated a physical attack, I find to avoid a prospective risk of harm, this matter would be reasonably resolved by the Appellant forgiving the loan to SC. There is no evidence on record that the Appellant's livelihood would be endangered by forgiving the loan. There is also no evidence that by doing so, the Appellant would be "required to compromise either who he is or a fundamental belief"14 nor would the Appellant be subjected to a risk to his life under subsection 97(1) of the Act.

Further, the assertion that SC has political influence and connections that have convinced the authorities to target and harm the Appellant if he does not withdraw his complaint, is speculative and unsubstantiated. I find there is insufficient evidence to establish that SC, the police, or politicians are conspiring to eliminate the Appellant "because his complaint raised the same issues as India's Leader of Opposition about 'the working of the judiciary and media, and the atrocities upon the poor and minority".15 The evidence indicates the Appellant continued to resend and forward the same complaint to various authorities, and it clearly focuses on SC's failure to repay a loan. I find any potential problems in India are related to the Appellant's unwillingness to forgive the loan.

The fact that the Appellant's complaints to the various authorities have not led to the outcome the Appellant had hoped for does not establish that these authorities are all colluding with SC to harm the Appellant. It is also notable that the Appellant remained in India, after filing his complaints, until XXXX2019, without any harm coming to him. Therefore, I find that the Appellant has failed to provide any persuasive evidence he would face, on a balance of probabilities, a forward-facing risk of torture, or a risk to life, or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, were he to return to India four years later.
I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD.

I find that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 of the Act as he has not established that he faces more than a mere possibility of persecution should he return to India. In addition, I find that the Appellant is not a protected person as per section 97(1) of the Act, as he has not established that he is a person in need of protection, in that his removal, would subject him personally to a danger of torture, a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment that extends throughout India.
